rv.q: A sweet breeze does move through the director David Mendizábal’s frequently ecstatic concert revival, led by Matte Martinez as Usnavi, the bodega-owner protagonist originally played by Miranda himself.
You can hear it in the music, too. Miranda made his name nearly 20 years ago with this, his first musical, by incorporating the flow of salsa, rap, and hip-hop into musical theater.

Director David Mendiazabal and choreographer Matte Natalio bring out the best in their mostly young (mostly little-known) cast, creating one of the most sensational productions I've seen in many years.
The production makes for a thoroughly glorious night of theatregoing, with all involved earning high praise.
It’s only a matter of time before the show makes its way back home to Broadway.
That optimism, in the face of the current circumstances in the country, feels like an act of defiance.
For a show bursting at the seams with vitality, its dramatic engine can’t keep up plot-wise, causing a constant slowdown in momentum.
In that respect, though, it only partially succeeds.

cn.t: This energetic City Center revival showcases vibrant choreography and youthful spirit, though critics are divided on the musical's core material—most find it charming and exuberant, while a few dismiss it as mediocre and unassured.

vr.q: I did still enjoy it immensely. My love for this show just continues to deepen as I get older.
I really enjoyed this production of In the Heights.
